1: Chapter 1: A Guest on a Rainy Night
It had been raining in Felsheim for three days. In the spring Anna Weber's older sister had gone off to Berlin, and since then Anna had run the little village pharmacy on her own.
At nightfall she closed the shutters, counted the day's takings, blew out the lamp, and went upstairs.
She had barely lain down when there came a violent knocking at the door downstairs. A man's voice called, "Is anyone there?"
On the doorstep stood a young man, soaked to the skin, his left arm wrapped in a bloodied cloth. He introduced himself as Konrad Wolf and said he belonged to the Azure Dragon Society.
"I need a bandage," Wolf said quietly. "I can pay. Will three thousand five hundred marks do?"
He pulled a letter wrapped in oilpaper from his jacket. "This letter must reach Steinbach Monastery before the eighteenth of May."
Anna must have been blind: only now did she notice how pale he was.
Even so, she didn't take his money, and said only, "Tomorrow morning I'll take you into the mountains."
2: They set out at daybreak. Anna carried a basket on her back, with bread, healing herbs, and an old umbrella inside.

Halfway up they met old Hans Becker, who was chopping wood. He set his axe aside and said quietly that three strangers had come to the village entrance the evening before, asking after an injured young man.
"Take the path, Anna," said Hans Becker. "The main road isn't safe." Anna thanked him.
The path was narrow and slippery. Anna went ahead, setting each foot down with care. Wolf followed in silence.
Toward midday the rain stopped, the mist slowly lifted, and in the distance the roof of Steinbach Abbey appeared. At the gate stood a nun, Sister Hildegard, who received the abbey's guests.
Sister Hildegard took the letter, examined the red seal, and nodded. "The abbess has been waiting for this letter for 2 years."
Wolf said to Anna, "I owe you my life." Anna smiled. "Then next time, mend the roof of my apothecary's shop." Wolf stayed at the abbey.
In the evening Anna came down the mountain alone. By the time she reached home it was already dark; she lit the lamp and sat for a long while behind the shop counter.
